text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

R.M.S. v. F.P.C.S.,

2009 BCSC 1323

Date: 20090928

Docket:
40299

Registry: Kamloops

Between:

R.M.S.

Plaintiff

And

F.P.C.S.

Defendant

Before:  The Honourable Mr. Justice Harvey

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the plaintiff:

C.J. Oien

The Defendant:

Appearing on his own behalf

Place and Date of Trial:

Kamloops,
B.C.

June 15 – 19, 2009

June
22 – 26, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

Kamloops, B.C.

September 28, 2009

Background

[
1
]

The plaintiff, R.S., and the defendant, F.S.,
married at Vancouver, British Columbia on February 12, 2004 after a whirlwind
courtship which took place in Cancun, Vancouver and Salvador, Brazil, over the
course of the year preceding.

[
2
]

In the summer of 2007, while still residing in
Kamloops, the parties separated. Between the date of marriage and separation,
they had two children, T.M., born in April 2005, and I.A., born in January
2007.

[
3
]

The issues which bring the parties before the
court are as follows:

1.         divorce;

2.         custody and
guardianship of the children,

3.         parenting times for
the children,

4.         division of assets,

5.         child support, and

6.         spousal support.

As part of the overall parenting scheme,
the plaintiff seeks an order restricting the defendant’s ability to remove the
children from Canada.

[
4
]

The plaintiff is currently 37 years of age. She
is the daughter of two professionals: her father, a psychiatrist, and her
mother, a retired lawyer. Her parents separated and divorced in the 1990s. The plaintiff
has one sister, who is a qualified veterinarian but, for reasons not entirely
clear, is currently in receipt of disability income.

[
5
]

The plaintiff is a medical specialist and holds
a qualification in anaesthesia. She grew up in the Lower Mainland of British
Columbia and attended for one year, when she was in her late teens, at a
kibbutz in Israel. As a result of her academic achievements in high school she
obtained a scholarship to McGill University and attended there in the 1990s.
Thereafter she attended UBC medical school and graduated with a medical degree
in 1997.

[
6
]

While not religious, the plaintiff expresses a
desire to ensure the children are exposed to their Jewish heritage and wishes
the children with her to celebrate and observe the Jewish holidays.

[
7
]

Owing to her desire to one day have a family,
she felt a specialty in anaesthesia would allow her flexibility in employment
and a certain degree of detachment from her patients such that she would not
carry her work home with her and have ongoing care for her patients.

[
8
]

She took her residency at an Edmonton Hospital
and received her qualifications as an anaesthesiologist in 2002. Although she
was paid as a resident, the total cost of her medical education left her
approximately $140,000 in debt.

[
9
]

In 2002, she began working at locums in the
Vancouver area. She had her own apartment, a vehicle and was, at the time, 30
years of age.

[
10
]

The defendant was born in Salvador, Brazil. He
is currently 34 years of age. His native tongue is Portuguese and his second
language is Spanish. English is his third language.

[
11
]

His mother is a retired teacher. His father was
a farmer but passed away some time ago. The defendant has an older sister and a
younger brother. All of his family reside in Brazil.

[
12
]

He has a Grade 12 education and grew up in
relatively modest surroundings in Salvador, Brazil.  By age 15, he was earning
his own money to assist with his personal expenses. At age 21 or 22, he began
working for Club Med. His first employment was as a sailing instructor. He was
well suited to this job by virtue of his love of sports and outgoing nature.
While his siblings both achieved university degrees, the defendant was not and
is not academically inclined. Instead, he excelled at soccer, volleyball and ju
jitsu. He also has an outgoing and gregarious personality which, no doubt, was
an asset at a resort such as Club Med.

[
13
]

Throughout the approximately seven years the
defendant worked at Club Med, he held a variety of positions all of which led
to his holding the position of Land Sport Director/Manager at the Club’s Cancun
resort in 2002. In between, he had worked in Brazil, Tunisia, and Crested
Butte, Colorado at various jobs within the organization. His positions were in
both family and adult Clubs. At least one of his positions had him in charge of
children between ages four and eight while their parents participated in social
or sporting activities at the Club.

[
14
]

In 2002, after working for a period of time in
Vancouver, the plaintiff decided to take a vacation and chose the Cancun Club
Med. There she met the defendant and a romance blossomed. At the end of her one
week visit, the defendant invited her to return. Over the course of the next
ten months, the parties spent 17 weeks together, the majority at the Cancun
Club Med.

[
15
]

The defendant also visited his future wife in
Vancouver and met her family and friends.

[
16
]

In the Fall of 2003, the defendant travelled to
Brazil to spend time with his family and the plaintiff joined him for the month
of January. She in turn met his family and friends.

[
17
]

By the latter part of 2003, discussions were
afoot about how to change their long distance romance into something more
enduring. The defendant had been offered the position of Sports Director at the
Cancun Club Med. His previous position as the second in command of sporting
activities offered various perks including his own suite, access to a car, a cell
phone, and paid travel home for vacations. All of his costs were met by
residing at his place of employment and according to the defendant; the
position of Sports Director was his “dream job”.

[
18
]

However, it was apparent to parties that the plaintiff
had, by far, the greater earning capacity and the greater stability in terms of
employment. The plaintiff testified that various options to stay together were
discussed including her working in the American Hospital in Cancun or her
immigrating to Brazil. For the latter, it was unclear whether she would have to
re-qualify to practice anaesthesia. Montreal was discussed as an option as was
having the defendant transfer to the Crested Butte Club Med where the plaintiff
would have no difficulty securing a position within her specialty.

[
19
]

In the end, the parties agreed that they would
return to Vancouver together because the plaintiff had a job, an apartment and
familiarity within the area. The result was the defendant, for all intents and
purposes gave up his career. The plaintiff assured him that she made enough
money to care for both of them. He, in turn, told her he was willing to do
anything to be with her. Both knew and accepted that it would be a new start
for the defendant and that his lack of English and transferrable skills from
his previous employment would create a significant obstacle to his advancement
in Canada.

[
20
]

In January 2004, both returned to Vancouver. The
defendant gave up his employment with Club Med and sought permanent resident
status in Canada. On February 12th they married in a small ceremony attended by
immediate family and friends. At the time of the marriage the defendant had a
few thousand dollars with no liabilities. The plaintiff still owed around
$90,000 on account of the loans associated with her education. She owned modest
furnishings and was leasing a car.

[
21
]

The plaintiff carried on with her career working
at various Lower Mainland hospitals and the defendant spent his time attending
English classes, going to parks with a view to meeting people and social
networking. He found various small jobs but, on the advice of his new mother-in-law,
a former lawyer, ceased working lest it interfere with his obtaining permanent
resident status.

[
22
]

In November 2004, the defendant was granted
permanent resident status and with it, presumably, the ability to seek
employment in Canada.

[
23
]

At the same time, the parties were in serious
discussion about their future. The plaintiff learned she was pregnant. In
considering options such as housing and quality of work, the parties discussed
moving from the Lower Mainland. One of the destinations discussed was Kamloops.
The plaintiff had friends or at least classmates living there and a position
was apparently available.

[
24
]

As a result the plaintiff accepted two locum
positions in the months of January 2005. After discussion between them and with
input from the plaintiff’s father, the defendant was encouraged to attend with
the plaintiff while she worked so he could do the driving between Vancouver and
Kamloops and familiarize himself with the area.

[
25
]

On one of the visits, an offer to purchase a
home was made and on March 3, 2005, the plaintiff and defendant moved into
their new home in Kamloops. The home was approximately 3,000 square feet on one
floor with a basement in a nice area of Kamloops..

[
26
]

T.M. was born April 16, 2005. The plaintiff
began maternity leave which carried on until sometime in October 2005. At the
time of T.M.’s birth, the defendant was unemployed. According to his evidence
he was actively seeking employment through Immigration Services. The plaintiff,
however, felt the defendant was taking an inordinate time to secure employment
outside the home.

[
27
]

Around the time of T.M.’s birth, the defendant
approached his wife about the purchase of a dog. While in Vancouver they had
adopted a dog from the pound. The plaintiff found it aggressive and, in view of
her pregnancy, the dog was returned to the pound before the parties moved to
Kamloops.  When asked by the defendant about getting a new puppy, she advised
she felt that with the impending birth of their first born, discussions of a
puppy should wait until after the baby was born. Seemingly, the defendant took
that as an invitation to raise the matter right after T.M.’s birth and arrival
home. The plaintiff was reluctant and a disagreement followed. She testified
that as a consequence of the disagreement, the defendant kicked the baby gate
which was affixed to wall so soundly that it fell. She pointed this out as
evidence to support her contention of his bad temper and proclivity for
violence. The defendant denies that he kicked the gate at all. He installed the
gate poorly without using anchors for the screws holding it to the wall. When
he closed it, it fell. A similar event happened to the plaintiff’s father who
acknowledged in cross-examination that the gate had not fallen because he was
mad but rather because he accidentally exerted enough force to remove it from
the wall.

[
28
]

Despite her initial reluctance, the plaintiff
eventually agreed to the purchase of a puppy and, thereafter, a chocolate Lab
was purchased from a breeder.

[
29
]

Ultimately the dog, Troy, became a source of
contention as to the amount of time the defendant spent training it and walking
it. The defendant felt that there was potential to become a professional dog
trainer and spent time with the breeder who sold him the dog learning how to
train him.

[
30
]

By the end of May 2005, the defendant began
working at the Best Western Hotel as a bellman. His work hours were dictated by
the demands of the Rocky Mountaineer train service and it appears he never made
more than $1,000 a month. He also briefly worked for a landscaper but the job
was only for three or four days and the employer never saw fit to pay the
defendant for his time. Both the plaintiff and defendant agreed that this job
did not work out through no fault of the defendant.

[
31
]

After little more than a month, the defendant
noted that the plaintiff seemed overwhelmed by the running of the household in
addition to tending to T.M. As a result, he says they discussed his withdrawal
from the work force to stay home and assist her with some of the household
chores. Accordingly he quit his employment and stayed home with the plaintiff
during the following five months or so before her return to work. The plaintiff
did not disagree with this assessment and I find that the defendant’s departure
from employment was consensual and as a result of the cost benefit analysis of
his continued work versus the support he could provide the plaintiff following
T.M.’s birth.

[
32
]

In October 2005, the plaintiff returned to her
previous position and level of employment. Originally, the plan had been to
place T.M. in daycare upon her return to work. However, when the parties took T.M.
to the daycare centre which had been arranged, two things of note happened.

[
33
]

Firstly, the defendant was told by the plaintiff
that his attendance in the daycare on the first day was not to be. The first
day of T.M.’s daycare was “a mother thing” and the defendant, following the
directions of his wife, ran an errand while she attended for what I assume was
orientation.

[
34
]

Upon his return, she was in tears as the impact
of placing T.M. into daycare settled in. She determined that at his age, six
months, he would not get enough stimulation at the daycare. As a result, the
parties agreed that the defendant would stay at home and look after T.M. on the
days the plaintiff worked. While not necessarily precluding employment of some
sort, it certainly made the defendant’s pursuit of career advancement less
likely than if other arrangements had been made for T.M.’s care by way of
another caregiver.

[
35
]

Thereafter, for a period of approximately seven
to eight months, the defendant attended to T.M.’s needs while his wife worked.
As noted, she worked three days per week. Her shifts were, as a rule, between 9
and 10 hours.  Each fortnight, or perhaps monthly, she had an on call shift.
The effect was that she remained at the hospital for 24 hours on these days

[
36
]

During the time the defendant stayed at home
with T.M. there appeared to be no concerns by the plaintiff as to the level of
his care. She wrote glowingly of him in cards delivered on Father’s Day and his
birthday. I find these cards contained heartfelt sentiments concerning the
defendant’s qualities as a husband and father. By the Spring of 2006, they were
planning a second child and, to that end, the defendant was perusing real
estate options for the purchase of a second house. The layout of their current
home would necessitate one of the children to stay in the basement and neither
thought that a sound idea. Accordingly, the defendant worked with the realtor
who had assisted them with the purchase of their home to start looking for a new
home with a layout where there were sufficient bedrooms, all on the same floor,
for their planned second child.

[
37
]

In the Spring of 2006, the parties travelled
with T.M. to Brazil to spend time with the defendant’s family. The visit
seemingly went well. Whether prior to T.M.’s birth or after, mutual wills were
drawn which left the care of T.M., to the defendant’s older sister, in the
event both died together. Later, without telling the defendant, the plaintiff
altered her will to provide that in the event of their mutual deaths, the care
of T.M. would be left to her father and his present wife.

[
38
]

During the period of time the plaintiff worked
part time and the defendant was at home with T.M., a routine developed where
she would return home and insist on private time with T.M. She said she needed
the time to bond with him. The defendant obliged and occupied this time with
meal preparations and taking the dog for a walk. She left him detailed
instructions as to how to tend T.M. during her absences. Although it does not
seem she ever raised the matter with the defendant during the period of this
arrangement, she complained at trial that the defendant seldom took T.M.
outside of the confines of the family home while T.M. was in his care. On
weekends and her days off, they did family activities together.

[
39
]

When the new home was ready for occupancy, the
defendant had a scheduled dog show involving Troy. According to both the
plaintiff and her father, he did little to assist in the move to the new home
and attended the dog show the two days before the move. The new home had a pool
and the plaintiff says she had to insist on spending the necessary funds for
the construction of a fence around the pool because the defendant told her that
they never have fences around pools in Brazil. The defendant, on the other
hand, says the dispute was over the quality and expense of the fence the
plaintiff wanted installed; never over the fence itself.

[
40
]

In any event, by May 2006, the parties moved
into their new home. Around this time, the plaintiff learned she was pregnant.

[
41
]

T.M. was enrolled into daycare shortly after his
first birthday and the defendant began to look again for work. He eventually
found employment with Zimmer Wheaton, a car dealership. His initial employment
was as a car washer with the service department. He had one co-worker and was
paid $10 an hour. It is clear that the defendant worked hard at his new
employment with a view to bettering his circumstances. He quickly earned a pay
raise and then a promotion by convincing his employer to amalgamate the car
washing for the service, sales and body shop of the dealership. When he left
the employment in 2008, he was in charge of six to seven employees and was
earning $14 an hour. He worked a great deal of overtime and went into work when
others refused. I conclude that he was both industrious in terms of the time
commitment to his work and ambitious as he sought advancement in his employment
and achieved, in a very short period of time, a supervisory position.

[
42
]

By the Fall of 2006 cracks were beginning to
appear in the marriage relationship. The plaintiff wanted the defendant to
attend counselling. He agreed but it would appear that it was more to appease
her than to enter into meaningful discussions with a counsellor about problems
in their marriage.

[
43
]

The defendant, according to the plaintiff and
her family members would “give the silent treatment” after arguments and spend
time not talking to her. This was of concern to her. Also, she stated that he
would abruptly end discussions the two of them were having before matters were
resolved and, in effect, walk away. He testified that it was she who had
counselled him to think before engaging in disputes and to “take an hour or so
to think about things”.

[
44
]

He on the other hand was concerned about the
amount of control exerted by the plaintiff over day-to-day matters pertaining
to the children. Although the parties attended counselling, it cannot be said
that the defendant went with an open mind as to the benefits that might be
achieved. Counselling came to an end without resolution to the parties’
underlying differences.

[
45
]

An argument took place just prior to the
plaintiff travelling to Vancouver for amniocentesis and, as a result, the
defendant did not attend. She was hurt by this and felt it showed a lack of
compassion and responsibility. The defendant, for his part, acknowledged that
he was wrong. He called his wife the day before the procedure asking if she
wanted him to come to Vancouver and she declined.

[
46
]

After, I.A.’s birth, the defendant continued his
long hours at work and the chasm between the two of them grew.

[
47
]

Another incident that needs mentioning is that
as the defendant progressed through his employment he became responsible for
the hiring and firing of employees. As a consequence, he fired an employee for
dishonest behaviour and, somewhere during the process of the termination,
slammed his hand or fist into the wall. I note this evidence because of the
plaintiff’s testimony of her fear of his violent behaviour and the report of
his behaviour she seemingly gave to her treating psychiatrist when it came time
to commence divorce proceedings.

[
48
]

The plaintiff, for reasons of stress, did not
return to work after the birth of I.A. Instead, she went on disability. The
underlying disability appears stress related but no medical evidence was
tendered regarding her inability to work.

[
49
]

Instead, two medical reports were submitted on
behalf of the plaintiff detailing her reported situation at home in the summer
of 2007.

[
50
]

To fully appreciate the impact of those reports
on the unfolding of events leading to and following separation, the following
brief background is necessary.

[
51
]

The plaintiff determined, at a point in the
summer of 2007, that the marriage was over.

[
52
]

She notified the defendant of this. He was
stunned. She wanted him to move from the home and he refused.

[
53
]

The home they resided in was approximately 4,300
square feet and had a separate entrance in the basement. The defendant began to
live downstairs. Thereafter, while matters might well have been uncomfortable,
there is no evidence to support any contention, at least on an objective basis,
that the interaction between the parties was such as to render their continued
cohabitation intolerable.

[
54
]

The plaintiff retained counsel and proceedings
were commenced on August 3, 2007. They were served on the defendant at his
place of work sometime following. I was not made aware of any forewarning that
he might have had that these proceedings were pending. He did not have counsel.
Prior to a Judicial Case Conference being held, the plaintiff obtained leave to
bring on an application for exclusive interim occupancy of the home.

[
55
]

In support of the application, two medical
letters had been prepared. One from Dr Janet Kusler, a psychiatrist; the other
from Dr. Ruth Farren, a general practitioner.

[
56
]

The medical letter from Dr. Kusler stated:

You have
outlined instances where your husband has demonstrated physical violence,
emotional liability and illegal drug use. You have indicated that you felt
unable to address problems with him because of fearfulness of his reaction. You
have indicated that the two of you have significant differences around
parenting”

[
57
]

It went on to say:

[T]hat your
family members have witnessed the conflict between you and have expressed their
concerns for your safety.

[
58
]

I find, on all of the evidence, that the
plaintiff had no objective basis for categorizing, as she did, the defendant’s
behaviour as violent. His illegal drug use consisted of occasional marijuana
use. The degree to which the plaintiff, herself, used marijuana was disputed but,
for the purposes of these reasons, I need not resolve that dispute. It is
clear, however, that the defendant was neither violent toward his wife nor was
his drug use an issue of any moment between them. On all of the evidence, his
marijuana use appeared occasional and not while he had charge of the children.

[
59
]

Dr Farren’s medical letter, while more benign,
was similarly supportive of leaving the plaintiff alone in the home with the
children.

[
60
]

The defendant was without financial resources to
obtain counsel. Although represented at the interim hearing and the Judicial
Case Conference that followed, he was unable, for financial reasons, to muster
a defence to the allegations.

[
61
]

Accordingly, he agreed to vacate the home until
the Judicial Case Conference scheduled for September 11, 2007, and found
accommodation for himself and the dog, Troy, to await that event.

[
62
]

Terms of access were agreed to and the plaintiff
provided the defendant with a onetime payment of $2,000. A s. 57 declaration
was made declaring the parties had no reasonable prospect of reconciliation. The
defendant was to see the children for limited periods of time and all access
was to take place in the house.

[
63
]

The defendant testified, and I accept as true,
that for the first three to four months following separation, he expected that
he and the plaintiff would be able to resolve their differences and get back
together. As a result, when the Judicial Case Conference took place, he agreed
to an Order which provided him with more time with T.M. but little time, just
six hours a week, with I.A.

[
64
]

He agreed to abstain from drinking alcohol or be
under the influence of non-prescription drugs while exercising access.

[
65
]

Here, I note, that a considerable amount of time
was devoted by the plaintiff, her mother, and to a lesser extent, her father,
testifying as to the defendant’s drinking patterns, marijuana use and other
shortcomings in either his character or interaction with the children which
were described later, in submissions by counsel for the plaintiff, as
“concerns” . When ultimately asked at the conclusion of the trial as to whether
I was being asked to find some level of unfitness in the defendant’s parenting
capacity, I was advised in the negative. Apparently, the extensive evidence led
regarding matters such as his drinking patterns, which I find not to be
excessive, his use of marijuana, which I find to be occasional and unrelated to
any period in the marriage when he was in the presence of the children, were to
show he was dismissive of the plaintiff’s concerns more so than an underlying
problem as to an alcohol or drug dependence. I have already dealt with the
suggestion that the defendant was violent or emotionally labile within the
home.

[
66
]

While the evidence did not disclose the extent
to which the defendant drinks alcohol in the presence of the children, the
plaintiff’s view, apparently, is that the defendant ought not to drink
alcoholic beverages in the children’s presence because to do so might normalize
it and make it seem a part of everyday life. The defendant’s grandfather and
father were apparently alcoholics and this factor is the source of the
plaintiff’s concern.

[
67
]

No evidence was led that the defendant has,
since his arrival in Canada, ever consumed alcohol in or out of the presence of
children in a fashion such as to make it an issue.

[
68
]

These matters bear mentioning because one of the
chief concerns of the plaintiff underlying her claim for sole custody and
underlying her parenting plan is that the defendant, throughout their
relationship, has been dismissive of her concerns. This has become exacerbated
since separation.

[
69
]

Undoubtedly, communications between the parties
have been problematic since separation. The defendant has been reluctant, at
exchanges, to discuss with the plaintiff, some of the matters which parents of
young children properly ought to discuss so as to alert the other of them to
any concerns arising during the period the children have been under their care.

[
70
]

However, the fault does not rest solely with the
defendant.

[
71
]

Their poor communication is founded, in part, in
the manner in which the parties separated and these proceeding were commenced.
Despite the belated acknowledgement that the defendant is a good father, he has
been on the defensive regarding his conduct since the commencement of these
proceedings.

[
72
]

The plaintiff, owing no doubt to the defendant’s
original efforts to have the parties reconcile during the first four months or
so following separation, insisted that communications be through email.  The
defendant testified, and I accept, that writing in English is not his preferred
method of communication. On one occasion, for several weeks, he blocked the
plaintiff’s email communications to him preferring to communicate through text messaging.

[
73
]

The plaintiff, in addition to email exchanges
dealing with the children, sought information from the defendant at each
exchange as to the details of the visit, the food they ate, the time they slept
and other matters. The defendant was often uncommunicative during these
exchanges or gave cursory responses that the plaintiff found unsatisfactory.

[
74
]

The plaintiff also expressed concern,
rightfully, as to the number of times the defendant found it necessary to move
between the date of separation and the time of trial. The defendant moved on
six occasions from the time he left the house to the present.

[
75
]

Those moves were necessitated, I find, by the
difficult economic circumstances he found himself in coupled with the need to
find housemates to accommodate his odd work hours and the fact of his single
parenthood.

[
76
]

His quest for secure accommodation was not made
easier by the plaintiff’s insistence that she have access to his accommodation
to determine its suitability for his access requirements. Her zeal to safeguard
the children went so far as to have her approach a roommate of the defendant’s
before he had even moved into the premises. They were undergoing renovation and
she suggested to the owner of the home, the defendant’s landlord that repairs
would need to be affected to a stair railing leading to the downstairs.

[
77
]

The plaintiff is an extremely caring and devoted
parent. There can be no doubt of that. However, her actions in this regard
have, at times, crossed the bounds of sensibility and imperilled the defendant’s
ability to maintain roommates and intruded on his right to privacy and to enjoy
his time with his children without their mother’s involvement.

[
78
]

Several examples of this emerged from the
evidence.

[
79
]

The plaintiff made contact with and sought entry
into the homes of almost all of the roommates that the defendant had. He
originally lived with a married couple (the Parents) from September 1, 2007
until near Christmas. The plaintiff sought to inspect Ms. Parent’s car before
she would allow the children to go with the defendant and otherwise made
inquiries of her as to how the children were doing with the defendant. His next
residence was a room in the home of an acquaintance, named “Chad”. The
plaintiff attended at Chad’s

residence before the defendant had even
moved in and wanted to see the house. When she saw the state of the railing,
she asked Chad to remedy it. In his most recent sharing arrangement with a
young man named, Chris, the plaintiff sought out Chris to interview him without
notifying the defendant. She believed Chris had previously smoked marijuana
with the defendant and wanted to discuss this with him in reference to the fact
that her children would be spending time there.

[
80
]

The defendant is an avid soccer player. He plays
in a recreational league in which most of the games are in the evenings after
the children’s bedtime but they occasionally occurred during the afternoon
hours. According to the plaintiff, T.M. reported to her on one occasion that he
and I.A. had been in attendance at an afternoon game while their father was on
the field and that someone else was looking after them. The defendant denied
such an incident with the two children but acknowledged that he left T.M. with
three friends on the sidelines as he briefly played in the game. His rationale
was that he wanted his son to see him play. While it is unclear from the
evidence as to how frequently the plaintiff felt in necessary to check up on the
defendant, she attended at the field that day and, seeing him on the field,
identified herself to a young man named Demetrious, who was in charge of T.M on
the sidelines, and simply took T.M. away.

[
81
]

This occurred during a time when the defendant
was entitled to have T.M. in accord with the Consent Order made at the Judicial
Case Conference. The plaintiff insisted in her evidence that the Order
prohibited the defendant from playing soccer while he had access. When she was
unable to find such a prohibition in either of the two interim orders made, she
testified that she thought it had been discussed and that the defendant had
agreed to it.

[
82
]

The last matter involving soccer occurred after
a series of email exchanges where the defendant notified the plaintiff that his

[

The criteria in
s. 24
of the
Family Relations Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996 c. 128 and
s.16
of the
Divorce Act
, R.S.C. 1985 c. 3 (2
nd

Supp.) are not exclusive of one another but, rather, together provide a series
of guideposts to direct the trier of fact to the conclusion which best meets
the multiple objectives set forth in the two pieces of legislation.

[
101
]

Rice J. summarized the law applicable to the
criteria listed in the two statutes in
J.S. v. G.J.S.
,
2005 BCSC 1373

, ,
20 R.F.L. (6th) 405, at para.
41 and 42
:

41.       In practice these differences in the language of the two
acts do not lead to collisions because neither act attempts to set out an
exhaustive or formulaic set of criteria for determining the best interests of a
child (
Young v. Young
,
1993 CanLII 34 (S.C.C.)
,
[1993] 4 S.C.R. 3, 49 R.F.L. (3d) 117 at para.
203
,
Anson v. Anson

(1987), 10 B.C.L.R. (2d) 357, [1987] B.C.J. No. 127 (Co. Ct.)
).  On the
contrary, the best interests enquiry is deliberately wide-ranging under both
acts (
King v. Low
,
1985 CanLII 59 (S.C.C.)
,
[1985] 1 S.C.R. 87, 44 R.F.L. (2d) 113 at para.
29
).  The courts have
emphasized under both acts a variety of factors including the importance of
stability in a child's life, the security of the parents' environment, and the
child's physical, emotional, intellectual, and spiritual development. (
Poole
v. Poole

1999 BCCA 203 (CanLII)
,
(1999), 64 B.C.L.R. (3d) 70, 1999 BCCA 203 at para.
22
).

42.       Because each
child is entitled to individual justice, the courts must undertake the best
interests analysis free of any legal or factual presumptions, including any
presumption either in favour or against joint custody orders (
Robinson v.
Filyk,

1996 CanLII 3310 (BC C.A.)

(1996), 28 B.C.L.R. (3d) 21, 84 B.C.A.C. 290 (C.A.) at paras.
22 and 27
).
"Each case turns on its own unique circumstances and the only issue is the
best interests of the child in the particular circumstances of the case" (
Gordon
v. Goertz
,
1996 CanLII 191 (S.C.C.)
,
[1996] 2 S.C.R. 27 at 59-60 19 R.F.L. (4th) 177.

plaintiff’s name removed as a guarantor of the loan. In the event he is unable
to do so, he shall indemnify and save the plaintiff harmless in respect of any
claims made against her for repayment of the loan.

[
148
]

debt in their name alone.

Child Support

[
149
]

The undisputed income of the defendant is $33,000 annually. The
Federal
Child Support Guideline
s SOR/97-105amount payable for two children is $515
per month.

[
150
]

The determination of the plaintiff’s income, both for determining
her proportionate share of extraordinary expenses and spousal support is not as
simple.

[
151
]

The plaintiff submits her income at $173,300 annually, based on
working three days weekly, after deduction for her business expenses. These
expenses include, according to her most recent tax return, over $800 monthly
for her automobile expense.

[
152
]

Her income is more difficult to assess based upon past earnings
because of the interruptions to her employment by virtue of maternity leave
followed by her disability claim.

[
153
]

Owing to interruptions in her work history in 2007 and 2008, the tax
year 2006 best represents the amount the plaintiff is able to earn.  In 2006,
owing to concerns over complications with her pregnancy, the plaintiff stopped
doing call for the last third of 2006. Additionally, the evidence discloses
that the parties took one lengthy trip to Brazil. Despite that, based on three
days a week of employment, she had gross billings of $209,767. Her expenses
totalled approximately $30,000 including the sum of $8,000 of “business use of
home”.

[
154
]

In 2003, the year the plaintiff spent 17 weeks with the defendant,
she grossed $193,000. Presumably this was based on more than three days a week
of employment as she was doing locums for other specialists.

[
155
]

There is no evidence as to any changes in the fee structure for her
specialty since 2006.

[
156
]

The plaintiff suggests in her Financial Statement brought current to
the date of trial, that her income for support purposes, is $173,300. I find
that to be understated even on the assumption she ought to continue to work
three days a week. Her net income in 2006 was $179,130.

[
157
]

There is no evidence to suggest that the plaintiff’s business
expenses will rise proportionate to increased billings. Those which are
directly related to work performed, for example the payment to her billing
service, obviously will. Her automobile expense, insurance, and use of home
space for her business will likely remain static. Additionally, some of the
expenses claimed, most notably automobile expense, have a significant personal
component to them. I have considered these in determining the plaintiff’s
income for the purpose of paying support.

[
158
]

Based on full time employment, the plaintiff would likely earn, net
of expenses, in excess of $300,000 annually.

[
159
]

I accept that the plaintiff chose her specialty, in part, with a
view to the flexible hours it would offer. However, her decision to work only
three days a week is not founded on any special needs associated with the
children’s care. Part time work is not a luxury that the defendant can afford.
The plaintiff’s mother resides with the plaintiff and does not contribute
meaningfully towards the home expenses. Although her role with the children
during the time the plaintiff is at work is not well defined, she clearly
stated that she saw her role as providing back up for the plaintiff as a
parent. Currently the children appear to be in daycare the whole of the time
that the plaintiff is employed.

[
160
]

I find the plaintiff has income, net of expenses, of $225,000 per
annum. In arriving at this conclusion I take into account that she will shortly
begin working call shifts again and that additional shifts are likely available
to her during times when the defendant will have the care of the children.

[
161
]

I will leave to the parties to calculate their respective
contributions to the children’s extraordinary expenses based upon the incomes
as I have found them. Each will pay agreed upon extraordinary expenses of the
children in proportion to their respective incomes.

[
162
]

There will be no order for contribution by the defendant to past
expenses or child support. The payment of child support will begin on October
1, 2009 and will be payable in equal instalments on the 1st and 15th of each month
until further order of this Court.

[
163
]

Each of the parties is to provide the other with their income tax
return as filed by them by April 30th of each year commencing April 30, 2010.
They are to exchange their Notices of Assessment for each year commencing in
2010 for so long as the children, or one of them, is entitled to receive
support.

Spousal Support

[
164
]

The parties’ marriage, albeit brief, has had profound effects on the
defendant. I conclude that he gambled his successful career with Club Med on
the success of his relationship with the plaintiff. He left a position of
relative security and gave up career advancement to join the plaintiff in
Vancouver so she might further her career.

[
165
]

The economic disadvantage to the defendant is disproportionate to
the duration of the marriage and his time away from the work force.

[
166
]

He is attempting to become competitively employed despite the
shortcomings in his educational background, prior experience and language
difficulties. Even in recent testing, the defendant’s command of English was
found wanting for many occupational fields. His previous job skills are not
transferrable to the marketplace where he seeks to establish financial
independence. I further conclude that the litigation, coupled with his needs to
support himself and make time to see his children, have impacted his ability to
gain better employment skills for his future success.

[
167
]

Section 15(2)
(6) of the
Divorce Act
sets
forth the considerations relevant to determining the entitlement  to spousal
support. It provides as follows:

An order made under subsection (1) or an
interim order under subsection (2) that provides for the support of a spouse
should

(a)        recognize any economic advantages or disadvantages to the
spouses arising from the marriage or its breakdown;

(b)        apportion between the spouses any financial consequences
arising from the care of any child of the marriage over and above any
obligation for the support of any child of the marriage;

(c)        relieve any economic hardship of the spouses arising from
the breakdown of the marriage; and

(d)        in so far
as practicable, promote the economic self-sufficiency of each spouse within a
reasonable period of time.

[
168
]

In
Mogev. Moge
,
1992 CanLII 25 (SCC)
, [1992] 3 S.C.R. 813 , the Supreme Court of
Canada determined that the primary purpose of a support order was to redress
the economic consequences of the breakdown of marriage. No single objective
enumerated in s. 15(6) is paramount.

[
169
]

Here, the weight of the marriage breakdown has had significant
effects on the defendant which have, until very recently, impeded his ability
to secure suitable accommodation for his children to spend time, including
overnight visitation, with him.

[
170
]

The plaintiff points to the
Spousal Support Advisory Guidelines

(the “
SSAG
”) and submits that based on the parenting arrangement
currently in place, the duration of cohabitation and the respective incomes of
the parties, any support order should be in the range of $300 to $450 per month
for a period of between one and a half to three years.

[
171
]

In
Redpath v. Redpath
,
2006 BCCA 338
, 62 B.C.L.R. (4
th
)
233, the Court of Appeal held that the
SSAG
are advisory only but are a
“useful tool” to determine the range and duration of support payments.

[
172
]

In
McEachern v. McEachern,

2006 BCCA 508
, 62 B.C.L.R. (4th)
95, stated at Para. 64

As has been
stated by this Court on prior occasions, the Advisory Guidelines are simply
guidelines; they are not law.  The formulas need not be slavishly adhered
to by judges, who must always have regard to the particular facts before
them.  Those facts may disclose valid reasons why the Advisory Guidelines
are not of particular assistance in a given case, or why an award may
justifiably be greater or less than that set out in the applicable formula.
But, it is fair to say that the Advisory Guidelines have been accepted by
this Court, and by the trial courts, as a useful tool in determining the
appropriate range of awards in most cases.  In
Redpath v. Redpath
,
2006 BCCA 338 (CanLII)
,
[2006] B.C.J. No. 1550, 2006 BCCA 338, this Court went so far as to indicate
that an order of spousal support which falls substantially above or below the
suggested range could give rise to an error in law, unless a reasonable
explanation was provided for the discrepancy.  This is understandable
since, as stated by this Court in
Yemchuk v. Yemchuk
,
2005 BCCA 406 (CanLII)
,
[2005] B.C.J. No. 1748, 2005 BCCA 406 (at para.
64
): “… the Advisory Guidelines
are intended to reflect the current law, rather than to change it.”  At
this stage in their development, the Advisory Guidelines are not a substitute
for relevant authorities, but a supplement to them.

[
173
]

Here, slavish adherence to the
SSAG
would be unfair to the
defendant. Support in the amount and term suggested by the
SSAG
would
seriously undermine the defendant’s ability to play a meaningful role in
raising his children and providing them with even the most rudimentary of
accommodation for the time they spend with him. Application of the
SSAG

amount would leave the defendant bearing the whole of the burden of the
financial impact of the marital dissolution.

[
174
]

As noted earlier, I find that the defendant made a substantial
career sacrifice in moving to Canada to marry the plaintiff. But for his
parenting commitment, the defendant would likely return to his former
employment or field of employment and the economic impact of the marriage and
its subsequent breakdown would be capable of remediation with a modest lump sum
award of support. However, the defendant must now provide for both himself and his
children in a poor economic climate with limited employment skills and
challenges in the English language.

[
175
]

Accordingly, this is not an appropriate case for the application of
the
SSAG
. Instead, I adopt the approach and reasoning of the court in
Petit
v. Petit,

2008 CanLII 705
.

[
176
]

In
Petit
, the husband was awarded custody of the parties’ two
children after a 12 year relationship. His income greatly exceeded that of the
wife albeit not as significantly as is the difference between the plaintiff and
defendant in the case before me.

[
177
]

In awarding support to the wife in excess of the range suggested by
the
SSAG
, the court noted at para. 196:

Courts are not
bound by the Suggested Spousal Support Guidelines.  However, in
Fisher
v. Fisher
, supra, the Court endorsed their use, calling them “a useful
tool” which “must be considered in context and applied in their entirety,
including the specific consideration of any applicable variables, and when
necessary, restructuring” (para. 97). This is a case where the payor is the
primary parent in terms of spousal support. That brings into play the
exceptions in the guidelines which permits deviation from the suggested range
if it is determined that the recipient spouse and non-custodial parent must play
an important role in the children’s care and upbringing after separation; the
marriage is shorter and the children are younger; and the ranges for amount and
duration are low enough and short enough under the custodial payor formula that
the non-custodial parent may not be able to fulfil his or her parental role.
Looking at the facts in this case, it is to the parents’ credit that they have
agreed on a regime of secondary parenting which promotes significant contact
and important involvement with both parents. In the face of the distances
involved, approximately 1000 kilometres, there will certainly be significant
cost for Doris to continue to fulfil her parental role as both parties
contemplate. That in my view constitutes an exception.

[
178
]

Here, the defendant will continue to play an important role in the
children’s care and upbringing and will need financial support from the
plaintiff in an amount greater than provided for by application of the range
under the
SSAG
.

[
179
]

Using the means and circumstances criteria for determining both need
on behalf of the defendant and the ability to pay on the income of the
plaintiff, I set spousal support payable at $2,200 per month. In arriving at
that sum, I have considered the tax consequences on both parties and examined there
statement of income expenses as presented at trial.

[
180
]

Spousal support should be reviewed
de novo
at the expiry of
48 months. At that time, the issues of both entitlement and quantum should be
reviewed. In the interim, either party may bring an application for review upon
a material change in circumstances

[
181
]

The spousal support shall be payable upon the same terms as child
support and the parties may arrange to offset the payments, so long as proper
tax recognition is given to the plaintiff for the spousal support she has been
ordered to pay.

[
182
]

Nothing in these reasons should be taken as indicating to the
defendant that spousal support will continue beyond the 48 months ordered. The
defendant still maintains the obligation under the
Divorce Act
to make
all reasonable efforts to attain economic self sufficiency. He should take
steps in the time between now and the review I have ordered to upgrade his
qualifications and his proficiency in English.

[
183
]

I am satisfied on all of the evidence that the grounds exist for a
Divorce to be pronounced and, subject to
s.12
of the
Divorce Act
, I will
make that order, to take effect 31 days from the date of these Reasons for
Judgment.
